episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: Why should orthodontists individualize fees based on case complexity instead of charging one flat fee?
transcript_excerpt: Dr. Goodman explains that the traditional one-fee model where easy cases subsidize hard cases is outdated. An experienced orthodontist can assess complexity—such as an impacted canine requiring significant work versus a minor crowding case treatable in 10 months with aligners—and price accordingly. This approach is more fair to patients and reflects the actual time, difficulty, and transformational value of each case, similar to how other medical procedures vary in cost.

episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: How can new orthodontists entering a market decide whether to position as premium or budget providers?
transcript_excerpt: Dr. Goodman advises choosing either the highest or lowest fee positioning to establish clear identity and market grab. If going premium, practitioners must credibly communicate what differentiates their service—not superficial amenities but genuine clinical advantages. If charging lower fees, limitations should be placed upfront (e.g., including only one round of aligners with additional refinements charged separately) to avoid loss of patient confidence through unexpected fee increases later.

episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: What is Dr. Adam Goodman's approach to handling patient requests to lower quoted orthodontic fees?
transcript_excerpt: Dr. Goodman maintains his quoted fees and does not discount based on patient negotiation. He argues this is fair to all patients who sacrifice and meet the original fee without haggling, and some may take loans or work second jobs to afford treatment. He illustrates this principle with a thought experiment: if a patient wants $1,000 off a $7,000 fee, he would counter-offer $8,000 instead, demonstrating that price negotiation should not be unidirectional.

episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: Why do non-extraction orthodontic cases require longer-term retainer use compared to extraction cases?
transcript_excerpt: In non-extraction cases, the dental arch is expanded, which represents technically unstable movement because facial muscles, tongue, and lips naturally shape and maintain a set arch. Additionally, ligament fibers have memory. Extraction cases historically showed more stability over time. Modern patients are also more aware of maintaining perfect results due to high-definition photography and raised standards of care, making even minor shifting noticeable.

episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: How should orthodontists retreat patients who experienced relapse after failing to wear retainers?
transcript_excerpt: Dr. Goodman recommends offering a substantial goodwill discount to recently-treated patients who neglected retainer wear, as it was not intentional negligence and makes good business sense. However, patients who were treated by another orthodontist and later experience relapse should receive a normal full fee. In either case, if relapse is caught early, correction can be more limited and less expensive than the original comprehensive treatment.

episode_title: OM Ep. 187- The Truth About Orthodontic Pricing: Fees, Value & Handling Price Objections
question: Can Invisalign aligners complete complex orthodontic cases faster than traditional braces?
transcript_excerpt: When properly programmed using ClinCheck, Invisalign can be as fast or faster than braces because teeth follow the planned aligner sequence consistently. While braces show faster initial results, they require ongoing adjustments, bracket changes, and wire modifications due to human factors. Aligners move teeth predictably toward the programmed destination, making them more efficient overall—analogous to how a turtle beats a rabbit by staying focused on one path rather than changing course repeatedly.
